name: Class II Arterial Hemorrhage — Lower Extremity
steps: Apply tourniquet 2 to 3 inches above the wound, not over a joint.
Tighten until bleeding stops. Mark the time on the patient's forehead with a marker.
Elevate the limb above heart level if no suspected fracture.
Pack the wound with a hemostatic dressing if tourniquet cannot be placed.
Monitor distal pulse every 2 minutes. If lost, reassess tourniquet placement.
Keep patient warm. Hypothermia worsens coagulopathy.

cautions.sickle_cell: Sickle cell increases vaso-occlusive risk. Tourniquet ischemia time is more dangerous — reassess at 30 minutes. Monitor for vaso-occlusive crisis signs: severe bone pain, chest pain, priapism.
cautions.anticoagulants: Expect prolonged bleeding time. Apply additional wound packing layers. Do not remove tourniquet in the field.
cautions.diabetes: Impaired wound healing and neuropathy may mask pain. Do not use pain as a guide to tourniquet effectiveness. Check distal pulse directly.
cautions.hypertension: High blood pressure may sustain arterial bleeding despite tourniquet. Ensure tourniquet is fully occlusive — no distal pulse is the goal.

name: Class II Hemorrhage — Shoulder / Upper Extremity
steps: Apply direct pressure with a trauma dressing for 3 to 5 minutes.
Elevate the arm above heart level if possible.
If bleeding does not stop, apply a wound packing dressing with hemostatic gauze.
Secure the arm in a sling to reduce motion and rebleeding.
Monitor for signs of shock: tachycardia, pallor, altered consciousness.
For axillary wounds, use junctional tourniquet or axillary packing — standard tourniquet cannot be placed.

cautions.sickle_cell: Avoid prolonged cold packs — vasoconstriction can trigger vaso-occlusive crisis in the extremity.
cautions.anticoagulants: Wound packing is especially important. Plan for prolonged pressure application (10+ minutes).
cautions.diabetes: Peripheral neuropathy may reduce pain signals. Assess wound depth visually, not by pain response.
cautions.hypertension: Persistent bleeding despite pressure may indicate arterial involvement. Escalate to junctional tourniquet early.

name: Penetrating Chest Trauma — Tension Pneumothorax Risk
steps: Seal the chest wound with a vented chest seal (two-sided if available). Do NOT use occlusive seal alone.
Sit the patient upright at 45 degrees if conscious and breathing.
Monitor for tension pneumothorax: absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, worsening hypoxia, distended neck veins.
If tension pneumothorax suspected: needle decompression at second intercostal space, midclavicular line.
Do NOT remove objects impaled in the chest — stabilize in place.
Administer oxygen if available. Reassess every 5 minutes.

cautions.sickle_cell: Sickle cell increases risk of acute chest syndrome — respiratory symptoms can escalate rapidly. Prioritize oxygenation.
cautions.anticoagulants: Hemothorax risk is elevated. Expect more internal bleeding even with minimal external wound.
cautions.asthma: Bronchospasm may mimic or worsen tension pneumothorax. Administer bronchodilator if available before needle decompression.
cautions.hypertension: Aortic injury is a higher-probability concern. Treat for hemothorax alongside pneumothorax.

name: Abdominal Penetrating Wound — Evisceration
steps: Do NOT push protruding organs back. Cover with a moist sterile dressing.
Apply gentle pressure around (not over) the wound to limit contamination.
Position patient supine with knees slightly bent to reduce abdominal tension.
Do NOT give oral fluids — surgery will be required.
Monitor for signs of hemorrhagic shock. Maintain airway.
Apply an abdominal binder loosely over the dressing to hold it in place during transport.

cautions.sickle_cell: Sickle cell patients have impaired wound healing and increased infection risk. Minimize contamination.
cautions.diabetes: Higher infection and sepsis risk. Keep wound covered and clean.
cautions.anticoagulants: Internal bleeding may be significant even with small entrance wounds. Treat for shock proactively.
cautions.pregnancy: Position tilted 15 degrees left lateral to relieve aortocaval compression.

name: Traumatic Amputation — Partial or Complete
steps: Apply tourniquet immediately, as high on the limb as possible.
Mark tourniquet application time on forehead. Do NOT remove in the field.
Cover the stump with a sterile or clean dressing.
If partial amputation: do NOT complete the amputation. Immobilize in position of comfort.
Preserve the amputated part if recoverable — wrap in moist sterile gauze, place in sealed bag, then in cool water. Do NOT put directly on ice.
Treat aggressively for hemorrhagic shock. Two large-bore IV access if possible.

cautions.sickle_cell: Ischemia from tourniquet is especially harmful. Document time precisely. Vasocclusive crisis can occur in the contralateral limb.
cautions.anticoagulants: Despite tourniquet, oozing from wound edges will continue. Additional hemostatic dressings around the stump are essential.
cautions.diabetes: Do not rely on pain to assess tourniquet effectiveness — neuropathy may blunt sensation.
cautions.hypothermia: Patients in cold environments deteriorate faster. Cover patient aggressively.

name: Major Burns — Rule of Nines Assessment
steps: Remove patient from heat source. Do NOT remove clothing stuck to burns.
Cool the burn with cool (not cold) water for 10 minutes if within first hour. Stop if patient becomes hypothermic.
Cover burns with a dry sterile dressing. Do NOT use wet dressings for large burns — hypothermia risk.
Start IV fluid resuscitation if available: Parkland formula — 4 mL per kg per % TBSA for first 24 hours.
Assess airway: if facial burns, singed nasal hairs, or hoarse voice — airway edema is imminent.
Do NOT break blisters. Do NOT apply ice, butter, or toothpaste.

cautions.diabetes: Burns in diabetic patients heal poorly and have very high infection risk. Aggressive wound coverage.
cautions.sickle_cell: Fluid resuscitation may trigger acute chest syndrome. Monitor respiratory status closely.
cautions.anticoagulants: Wound bed may ooze more than expected. Monitor hemoglobin.
cautions.inhalation_injury: Priority: airway over wound. Early intubation if available.

name: Traumatic Brain Injury — Concussion to Severe
steps: Stabilize the cervical spine if mechanism suggests neck injury.
Assess GCS (eye, verbal, motor). GCS ≤ 8 = severe TBI — establish airway.
Apply pressure to scalp lacerations — scalp bleeds heavily.
Position head at 30 degrees elevation if no spinal injury suspected.
Do NOT administer opioids or sedatives — masks neurological status.
Monitor every 5 minutes for deteriorating consciousness, unequal pupils, vomiting.

cautions.anticoagulants: Intracranial hemorrhage risk is dramatically elevated. Any TBI in anticoagulated patient is high priority for evacuation.
cautions.diabetes: Hypoglycemia can mimic TBI. Check blood glucose if available.
cautions.hypertension: Maintain systolic BP > 90 mmHg to preserve cerebral perfusion pressure.
cautions.sickle_cell: Sickle cell increases stroke risk — TBI can trigger ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke in addition to direct trauma.

name: Tension Pneumothorax — Needle Decompression
steps: Identify: absent unilateral breath sounds, tracheal deviation away from affected side, distended neck veins, hypoxia, hypotension.
Needle decompression: 14-gauge angiocath at second intercostal space, midclavicular line, superior margin of the rib.
Advance needle until air rush is heard. Leave the catheter in place.
If vented chest seal present and applied, burp the valve to release pressure.
Reassess breath sounds. If no improvement, consider bilateral tension — decompress opposite side.
Place patient in position of comfort. Reassess every 5 minutes.

cautions.asthma: COPD/asthma can mimic tension pneumothorax. Administer bronchodilator first if tension signs are equivocal.
cautions.sickle_cell: Acute chest syndrome can present similarly. If no improvement after needle decompression, consider acute chest syndrome.
cautions.anticoagulants: Hemothorax may accompany pneumothorax — needle decompression risks hemothorax drainage into pleural space.
cautions.obesity: Deeper chest wall may require longer needle (3.25 inch). Standard 14g may not reach pleural space.

name: Hemorrhagic Shock — Class III/IV
steps: Control all visible bleeding immediately with tourniquets, pressure, and wound packing.
Lay patient flat. Elevate legs if no spinal injury suspected.
Establish IV access — two large-bore peripheral IVs if possible.
If available: transfuse packed red blood cells and plasma in 1:1 ratio. Do NOT infuse large volumes of crystalloid alone.
Keep patient warm — hypothermia worsens coagulopathy and mortality.
Reassess every 2 minutes. GCS, radial pulse, skin color.

cautions.sickle_cell: Sickle cell causes microvascular occlusion under hypoxia and hypotension — shock is rapidly life-threatening. Prioritize oxygenation alongside hemorrhage control.
cautions.anticoagulants: Coagulopathy is baseline — patient bleeds faster and clots less. Tranexamic acid (TXA) if available is critical.
cautions.diabetes: Autonomic neuropathy may blunt tachycardia as a shock marker. Rely on blood pressure and skin color instead.
cautions.pregnancy: Pregnant patients can lose 30-40% of blood volume before showing hypotension. Maintain left lateral tilt.

name: Airway Obstruction — Foreign Body or Swelling
steps: Position patient: chin lift / jaw thrust to open airway.
Inspect oral cavity for visible obstruction. Remove with finger sweep only if clearly visible.
Insert nasopharyngeal airway (NPA) if available and no head trauma.
If obstruction persists and unconscious: attempt bag-valve-mask ventilation.
If complete obstruction and unable to ventilate: surgical airway (cricothyrotomy) if trained.
Recovery position if breathing returns and no spinal injury suspected.

cautions.burns: Facial or inhalation burns cause rapid progressive airway edema. Act immediately — delay of minutes can make intubation impossible.
cautions.sickle_cell: Hypoxia from airway obstruction will trigger sickle cell crisis. Priority is oxygenation.
cautions.trauma: Assume cervical spine injury in all high-mechanism airway patients. Use jaw thrust, not head-tilt.
cautions.anticoagulants: Airway instrumentation may cause significant oropharyngeal bleeding. Suction must be available.

name: Long Bone Fracture — Femur / Tibia / Humerus
steps: Immobilize the fracture in the position found. Do not attempt to straighten angulated fractures.
For open fractures: cover bone/wound with sterile dressing. Do NOT push bone back in.
For femur fractures: apply traction splint if available — femur fracture can cause 1-2L internal blood loss.
Check and document neurovascular status (sensation, pulse, capillary refill) before and after splinting.
Pad all bony prominences under the splint.
Elevate the extremity above heart level to reduce swelling.

cautions.anticoagulants: Compartment syndrome and internal hemorrhage risk are elevated. Monitor for compartment syndrome signs: pain out of proportion, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesia, paralysis.
cautions.diabetes: Peripheral neuropathy can mask compartment syndrome. Monitor compartment pressure directly if possible.
cautions.osteoporosis: Fracture pattern may be more comminuted than expected. Immobilize a larger segment.
cautions.sickle_cell: Bone infarct is common in sickle cell and may mimic fracture. Bone pain + swelling without trauma = possible vaso-occlusive crisis, not fracture.

name: Anaphylaxis — Severe Allergic Reaction
steps: Administer epinephrine 0.3mg IM (EpiPen or auto-injector) to the outer thigh immediately.
Call for MEDEVAC — epinephrine is temporizing, not curative.
Position: supine with legs elevated unless respiratory distress, then sitting upright.
If wheezing: administer bronchodilator (albuterol) if available.
Monitor for biphasic reaction — symptoms can recur 1-8 hours after initial response.
Repeat epinephrine every 5-15 minutes if no improvement. Max 3 doses.

cautions.hypertension: Epinephrine will elevate blood pressure further. No dose reduction in anaphylaxis — epinephrine is life-saving. Administer standard dose.
cautions.heart_disease: Cardiac arrhythmia risk with epinephrine. Administer IM, not IV, to reduce peak concentration.
cautions.diabetes: Epinephrine causes hyperglycemia. Treat anaphylaxis first; manage glucose secondarily.
cautions.sickle_cell: Epinephrine-induced vasoconstriction can precipitate vaso-occlusive crisis. No dose modification — anaphylaxis is immediately life-threatening.
